primary.quote: Just prior to the time I left DEC in 1974 I remember Ken Olsen (president of DEC) saying that he couldn’t see any need or any use for a computer in someone’s home

popular_source.title: Wikiquote, William Thomson (notes the line is often reproduced without a primary source, citing Cerf and Navasky, The Experts Speak, 1984)

primary.quote: I have not the smallest molecule of faith in aerial navigation other than ballooning or of expectation of good results from any of the trials we hear of.

landed.record: No deadline stated. The letter expresses doubt about the trials then under way and gives no date or event.

popular_version: stock prices have reached 'what looks like a permanently high plateau.'

popular_source.title: Federal Reserve History, Stock Market Crash of 1929

primary.title: New York Times, 16 October 1929, p. 8 (page not fetched, cited by Federal Reserve History, which quotes it)
primary.quote: stock prices have reached 'what looks like a permanently high plateau.'
primary.note: Fisher spoke at the monthly dinner of the Purchasing Agents Association on 15 October 1929. The Times report is paywalled and was not read by us. The wording is the Federal Reserve's quotation of it.

landed.record: No deadline stated beyond 'permanently'. The Dow stood at 381 in September 1929, lost almost half its value by mid-November 1929, closed at 41 in summer 1932, and did not return to its pre-crash height until November 1954.

popular_version: I predict the Internet will soon go spectacularly supernova and in 1996 catastrophically collapse.

popular_source.title: Quote Investigator, 'I Predict the Internet Will Soon Go Spectacularly Supernova and in 1996 Catastrophically Collapse'

primary.title: InfoWorld, 'From the Ether: Predicting the Internet’s catastrophic collapse and ghost sites galore in 1996' by Bob Metcalfe, p. 61 (text as reproduced by Elon University Imagining the Internet, page scan not fetched)
primary.quote: But I predict the Internet, which only just recently got this section here in InfoWorld, will soon go spectacularly supernova and in 1996 catastrophically collapse.
primary.note: The popular version drops the clause 'which only just recently got this section here in InfoWorld'. Elon dates the column 1 December 1995, Quote Investigator 4 December 1995.

landed.record: InfoWorld of 28 April 1997 reports that Metcalfe put a copy of the column in a blender at a conference and ate it. The Economist covered the episode in April 1997 under the title 'Why the Internet failed to collapse'. We did not fetch a measurement of network outages for 1996.

summary: The words are in Metcalfe's 4 December 1995 InfoWorld column. He publicly ate the column in April 1997 after the Internet had not collapsed in 1996.

popular_version: The truth is no online database will replace your daily newspaper, no CD-ROM can take the place of a competent teacher and no computer network will change the way government works.

popular_source.title: Newsweek, 'Why the Web Won’t Be Nirvana' (the article itself)

primary.title: Newsweek, 'Why the Web Won’t Be Nirvana' by Clifford Stoll (online page, dated 26 February 1995)
primary.quote: The truth is no online database will replace your daily newspaper, no CD-ROM can take the place of a competent teacher and no computer network will change the way government works.
primary.note: The online page is Newsweek's own text of the piece. It also says 'Stores will become obselete' as one of the promises Stoll is doubting, and 'Baloney' and 'Bah' appear in the text.

landed.record: No deadline stated. The claims are open-ended ('will replace', 'will change') and we did not fix a test for each.

summary: The sentence is in Stoll's Newsweek piece of February 1995. It states no deadline, so it is not scored.

popular_version: by 1975 economics may dictate squeezing as many as 65000 components on a single silicon chip.

popular_source.title: Moore, 'Cramming More Components onto Integrated Circuits' (1998 Proceedings of the IEEE reprint), abstract

primary.title: Gordon E. Moore, 'Cramming More Components onto Integrated Circuits', Electronics, pp. 114-117 (copy: 1998 Proceedings of the IEEE reprint)
primary.quote: That means by 1975, the number of components per integrated circuit for minimum cost will be 65 000.
primary.note: The complexity for minimum component cost 'has increased at a rate of roughly a factor of two per year' and Moore says it can be expected to continue 'for at least ten years'.

landed.record: Moore's own 1975 paper plots a 16,384-bit charge-coupled-device memory chip as the 1975 point on the complexity curve and says annual doubling from 1959 gives about 65,000-fold growth. The text we read does not print the plotted component count for that chip, and we did not read the figure. In the same paper Moore revises the forward slope to a doubling about every two years by the end of the decade.

summary: Moore's 1965 article states 65,000 components per circuit by 1975. His 1975 paper plots a 16,384-bit memory chip as the 1975 point, but the plotted count is in a figure we did not read, so we do not score it.

popular_source.title: Brynjolfsson and McAfee, The Second Machine Age (2014), as quoted by Quote Investigator, dated 1965

who: Marvin Minsky (as reported by Brad Darrach in Life)
popular_version: In from three to eight years we will have a machine with the general intelligence of an average human being.

popular_source.title: Life, 'Meet Shakey' by Brad Darrach (scan hosted by gwern.net)

primary.title: Life, 'Meet Shakey, the First Electronic Person' by Brad Darrach (scan, text extracted)
primary.quote: In from three to eight years we will have a machine with the general intelligence of an average human being.
primary.note: Darrach writes that Minsky 'recently told me' this. The issue date is from Wikipedia's citation of the article. Darrach adds that others working in the field said 'give us 15 years'.
primary.archive_note: no capture made: Save Page Now was refused or timed out (Quote Investigator answers the Internet Archive crawler with 403) and no earlier capture exists

landed.record: We found no public record of a machine with the general intelligence of an average human being, as the Life article describes it, by November 1978. The 1973 Lighthill report on AI research says that 'In no part of the field have the discoveries made so far produced the major impact that was then promised'. That report predates the deadline by five years.

summary: The words are in the 20 November 1970 Life article, as reported speech by the journalist. Eight years from that date is November 1978, and no record of such a machine was found.

popular_version: The battle to feed all of humanity is over.

popular_source.title: The Population Bomb, Sierra Club-Ballantine edition (scan), Prologue

primary.title: Paul R. Ehrlich, The Population Bomb, Prologue (Ballantine paperback, first printing May 1968; scan copy, OCR text)
primary.quote: The battle to feed all of humanity is over. In the 1970’s the world will undergo famines—hundreds of millions of people are going to starve to death in spite of any crash programs embarked upon now.
primary.quote_ocr_note: The OCR text of the scan reads 'goin;' for 'going' and uses a different apostrophe. The wording is otherwise as printed.
primary.note: The same book also says 'But there will be famines' about the next decade or so.

landed.record: Our World in Data, using World Peace Foundation data, gives 36 million as the most likely death toll of the largest single famine in its record (China, 1958 to 1962), and says famine deaths in recent decades are low by historical standards. No famine in that record approaches hundreds of millions of deaths in the 1970s.

summary: The prologue of the 1968 book says hundreds of millions would starve in the 1970s. The largest famine toll in the dataset we read is about 36 million, in 1958 to 1962.

popular_version: The Simon–Ehrlich wager was a 1980 scientific wager between economist Julian Simon and biologist Paul Ehrlich, betting on a mutually agreed-on measure of natural-resource scarcity over the decade leading up to 1990.

popular_source.title: Wikipedia, Simon-Ehrlich wager

primary.title: John Tierney, 'Betting on the Planet', New York Times Magazine (contemporaneous report of the terms and result)
primary.quote: If the 1990 combined prices turned out to be higher than $1,000, Simon would pay them the difference in cash.
primary.note: Ehrlich's group chose chrome, copper, nickel, tin and tungsten, $200 of each at 1980 prices. The 1980 wager document itself was not found. Tierney's page was read through an Internet Archive capture.

earliest_found.title: Julian Simon, The Ultimate Resource (1981), cited by Wikipedia; not fetched

landed.record: Tierney: 'Each of the five metals chosen by Ehrlich's group, when adjusted for inflation since 1980, had declined in price.' Ehrlich's group predicted rising prices, so their side reads WRONG. Ehrlich mailed Simon a check for $576. Wikipedia gives 29 September 1990 as the payoff date and Tierney says October 1990.

summary: Ehrlich's group bet in 1980 that the inflation-adjusted prices of five metals would rise by 1990. All five fell and Ehrlich paid Simon $576.

popular_version: Hubbert correctly predicted that production of oil from conventional sources would peak in the continental United States around 1965–1970.

popular_source.title: Wikipedia, Hubbert peak theory

primary.title: M. King Hubbert, 'Nuclear Energy and the Fossil Fuels', American Petroleum Institute, Spring Meeting of the Southern District, San Antonio, 7-9 March 1956 (scan; text read by our own OCR)
primary.quote: the curve must culminate at about 1965 and then must decline at a rate comparable to its earlier rate of growth ... even then the date of culmination is retarded only until about 1970
primary.quote_ocr_note: The PDF is image-only. The text was produced by tesseract OCR run by us and saved as hubbert1956_ocr_tesseract.txt. This passage is for an assumed ultimate recovery of 150 billion barrels. For 200 billion barrels the paper says 'even then the date of culmination is retarded only until about 1970'.
primary.note: The paper is about crude oil production in the United States as then recoverable.

earliest_found.title: Nuclear Energy and the Fossil Fuels (API, March 1956)

landed.record: EIA annual U.S. field production of crude oil is 9,238 thousand barrels a day in 1969, 9,637 in 1970, the highest of the 1970s, and 9,463 in 1971. Production then fell and rose again, reaching 10,972 in 2018 and 12,335 in 2019, above the 1970 level. Hubbert's paper makes no claim about those later years or about shale.

summary: The 1956 paper puts the U.S. oil production peak at about 1965 on one assumption and about 1970 on another. EIA data show the peak at 1970 for that period. Output passed the 1970 level again in 2018.
